title: People missed that Jonah knew God would forgive—that’s why he ran (Jonah 4:2)
paragraphs: People missed that Jonah knew God would forgive—that’s why he ran (Jonah 4:2)

Jonah did not run because he doubted God’s power.
He ran because he knew God’s mercy.
That is the scandal in the story.

Most people preach Jonah like he was afraid of Nineveh.
But Jonah 4:2 pulls the mask off: he says he fled because he knew the Lord is “gracious and compassionate, slow to anger and abounding in love.” Jonah was not shocked by God’s judgment.
He was offended by God’s grace.

He wanted justice for them.
God wanted repentance for them.
And that is where the book stops being about Jonah and starts exposing us.

Because sometimes we do not struggle with God punishing evil.
We struggle with God forgiving the people we think deserve fire.

The real storm in Jonah was not only on the sea.
It was in the prophet’s heart.

But here’s what we miss: Jonah hated mercy for Nineveh, yet he was living on that same mercy himself. He wanted grace for his failure, but not for their repentance. That is the human heart apart from Christ.
And that is why we need Jesus.

Jesus is the better Jonah. Jonah ran from his enemies. Jesus walked straight toward His. Jonah sat outside a city hoping for judgment. Jesus wept over a city before bearing judgment Himself. Jonah was angry that sinners might be spared. Jesus shed His blood so sinners could be saved.

So yes—Jonah knew God would forgive.
That is exactly why he ran.

And maybe that is why this book still cuts so deep.
It reveals how easily we rejoice in grace for ourselves while resisting grace for others.

But the Gospel is bigger than our bitterness.
In Christ, even hearts like Jonah’s can be confronted, broken, and remade.
